M3-01-COSAENWC.2: In {B_NWC_CORR} compute Net Working Capital (NWC) for the CURRENT YEAR: trade receivables ({B_CREDITI_CORR}) plus inventory ({B_RIMANENZE_CORR}) minus trade payables ({B_DEBITI_CORR}). No number typed by hand: only the three references.
M3-01-COSAENWC.3: In {B_NWC_PREC} compute THE SAME Net Working Capital, but for the PREVIOUS YEAR: the formula is identical to the one above, only the data changes. Trade receivables ({B_CREDITI_PREC}) plus inventory ({B_RIMANENZE_PREC}) minus trade payables ({B_DEBITI_PREC}). You'll need it in the next level, to calculate how much NWC changed from one year to the next.
M3-01-COSAENWC.4:
## Net working capital, from its three pieces

In M1-07 you built the cash flow statement starting from a change in Net Working Capital (ΔNWC) that arrived ready-made, as a single signed number. That was a stated simplification: here, in M3, it gets taken apart. NWC (*Net Working Capital*, operating) no longer arrives ready-made — you build it yourself, from three trade items at period end:

> **Operating NWC = Trade receivables + Inventory - Trade payables**

**Note**: this is the OPERATING, trade definition — not the full accounting definition of working capital (which would also include accruals, prepayments and other current assets/liabilities not tied to the trading cycle). But it's exactly the definition used in practice in M&A when people talk about "NWC", and it's the one the rest of this module is built on.

**Why are receivables and inventory added, and payables subtracted?** Trade receivables and inventory are money the company has already "frozen" — sold but not yet collected, or bought but not yet sold. Trade payables are the opposite: money the company still has to pay its suppliers, so cash that hasn't left yet. More receivables and stock mean less cash available; more payables to suppliers mean more cash available — hence the sign.

Here you have data for two periods. Current year: trade receivables {p0}, inventory {p1}, trade payables {p2}. Previous year: trade receivables {p3}, inventory {p4}, trade payables {p5}.

Compute the NWC of both years, with the same formula. I'm not asking you yet to calculate how much it changed from one year to the next — that's the next level, where the two numbers you're about to calculate become the starting point. Just remember the rule you already know from M1-07: NWC that INCREASES absorbs cash, NWC that DECREASES releases it. Same sign, always.
M3-01-COSAENWC.14: ={B_CREDITI_CORR}+{B_RIMANENZE_CORR}-{B_DEBITI_CORR}: receivables plus inventory, minus trade payables.
M3-01-COSAENWC.15: ={B_CREDITI_PREC}+{B_RIMANENZE_PREC}-{B_DEBITI_PREC}: same formula as above, applied to the previous year's data.
M3-01-COSAENWC.title: What net working capital (NWC) is
M3-02-DSODIODPO.2: In {B_DSO} compute DSO (Days Sales Outstanding): how many days, on average, the company takes to collect its sales. Formula: trade receivables ({B_CREDITI}) divided by annual revenue ({B_FATTURATO}), times 365 (the days in a year). 365 is the only number you type by hand: the rest are references.
M3-02-DSODIODPO.3: In {B_DIO} compute DIO (Days Inventory Outstanding): how many days, on average, goods sit in the warehouse before being sold. Formula: inventory ({B_RIMANENZE}) divided by annual cost of goods sold — COGS — ({B_COGS}), times 365. Same structure as the previous task, only the items change: revenue has nothing to do with it here, because inventory is valued at cost, not at selling price.
M3-02-DSODIODPO.4: In {B_DPO} compute DPO (Days Payable Outstanding): how many days, on average, the company takes to pay its suppliers. Formula: trade payables ({B_DEBITI}) divided by annual purchases from suppliers ({B_ACQUISTI}), times 365. Note the denominator: it's not the COGS from the previous task, it's purchases — the item supplier payables really come from.
M3-02-DSODIODPO.5: In {B_CCC} compute the Cash Conversion Cycle: DSO ({B_DSO}) plus DIO ({B_DIO}) minus DPO ({B_DPO}). Don't recompute anything from scratch: you've just found the three numbers, this task is only about combining them. A positive CCC is days of cash "frozen" in the operating cycle — the time between when the company has to pay to produce/buy and when it collects from customers again. DPO is SUBTRACTED because it's the only one of the three that works in favour of cash: until the company pays its suppliers, it's as if they were lending it the money. More DPO, less capital it has to advance out of its own pocket — the same sign already seen in M3-01, where trade payables were subtracted from NWC.
M3-02-DSODIODPO.6:
## The Cash Conversion Cycle: DSO, DIO, DPO

In M3-01 you built NWC from three period-end items: receivables, inventory and trade payables. You knew HOW MUCH each was worth, but not how big it was relative to the business volume that generates it. That's what this level adds: the same three items, read as a number of DAYS.

> **DSO** = Trade receivables / Revenue × 365 — average days to collect sales
> **DIO** = Inventory / COGS × 365 — average days goods stay in the warehouse
> **DPO** = Trade payables / Purchases × 365 — average days to pay suppliers

> **Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) = DSO + DIO − DPO**

The CCC measures how many days pass, on average, between the moment the company lays out cash (to produce or buy goods) and the moment it collects it again from customers. DSO and DIO are both days in which cash has already gone out — or not yet come in — but isn't available: they're added. DPO is the opposite: they're the days in which SUPPLIERS are financing the company, because it hasn't paid them yet — that's why it's SUBTRACTED. It's the same sign you already used in M3-01, where trade payables were subtracted from NWC: more payables (or more DPO), less cash the company has to advance out of its own pocket.

The year's data: revenue {p0}, cost of goods sold (COGS) {p1}, purchases from suppliers {p2}. At period end: trade receivables {p3}, inventory {p4}, trade payables {p5}.

Note that purchases and COGS do NOT match ({p6} against {p7}): in reality they differ by the change in inventory during the year. Use the right denominator for each ratio, as indicated in each task.

Compute DSO, DIO and DPO one at a time (tasks 1-3), then combine them into the Cash Conversion Cycle (task 4).
M3-02-DSODIODPO.7: The Cash Conversion Cycle: DSO, DIO, DPO
M3-02-DSODIODPO.title: The Cash Conversion Cycle: DSO, DIO, DPO
M3-03-NWCEFCF.2: In {B_DNWC} compute the change in NWC (ΔNWC) over the period: closing NWC ({B_NWC_CHIUSURA}) minus opening NWC ({B_NWC_APERTURA}). Watch the order: closing minus opening, not the other way round — it's the sign that decides, in the next task, whether NWC absorbed or released cash.
M3-03-NWCEFCF.3: In {B_FLUSSO_NETTO} compute operating cash flow NET of the NWC effect: gross flow ({B_FLUSSO_LORDO}) minus the ΔNWC just calculated ({B_DNWC}). It's exactly the same sign already used in M1-07 for ΔNWC: a POSITIVE ΔNWC means NWC increased and ABSORBED cash, so it's subtracted from the gross flow. A NEGATIVE ΔNWC means NWC decreased and RELEASED cash: subtracting a negative number gives it back, and the net flow comes out higher than the gross. It's not a new sign to learn: it's the same as always.
M3-03-NWCEFCF.4:
## NWC and Free Cash Flow: the change that eats (or releases) cash

In M1-07 the change in Net Working Capital (ΔNWC) arrived as a single signed number, ready to be subtracted in operating cash flow — a simplification stated in that level. In M3-01 and M3-02 you already learned to build NWC from receivables, inventory and trade payables, and to read it in days with DSO/DIO/DPO: that part isn't repeated here. This level takes the step M1-07 took for granted: start from an OPENING and a CLOSING NWC for the period, and actually build their difference.

> **ΔNWC = Closing NWC − Opening NWC**
> **Operating cash flow, net of the NWC effect = Gross flow − ΔNWC**

**The sign, again, isn't new.** NWC that INCREASES during the period has ABSORBED cash: the company has "frozen" more money in receivables and stock than it has freed up through supplier payables — that's why ΔNWC is SUBTRACTED from the gross flow. NWC that DECREASES has RELEASED cash: subtracting a negative ΔNWC gives it back, and the net flow comes out higher than the gross. It's exactly the sign already used in M1-07 for ΔNWC: here you prove it from scratch, starting one level of detail further upstream, instead of just quoting it.

Opening NWC for the period: {p0}. Closing NWC for the period: {p1}. Gross operating cash flow for the year, BEFORE the NWC effect: {p2}.

First compute ΔNWC, then use it to get to operating cash flow net of the NWC effect. Two steps, a single sign to respect for both.

M3-04-CAPEXMAINTENANCEGROWTH.2: In {B_CAPEX_MANT} estimate the year's MAINTENANCE capex using the convention stated in the brief: in the long run maintenance capex tends to converge towards the year's depreciation (D&A), so use D&A ({B_DA}) directly as the estimate. It's not an accounting law, it's a reasonable approximation when the detail isn't available.
M3-04-CAPEXMAINTENANCEGROWTH.3: In {B_CAPEX_CRESCITA} compute GROWTH capex: the year's total capex ({B_CAPEX_TOTALE}) minus the maintenance capex just estimated ({B_CAPEX_MANT}). Careful how you read it: high growth capex is NOT a problem in itself — it's discretionary, and should be judged on the expected return of that expansion, not feared because it's a big number. Maintenance capex, on the contrary, isn't negotiable: cutting it doesn't reduce future growth, it reduces the productive capacity the company already has today.
M3-04-CAPEXMAINTENANCEGROWTH.4:
## Maintenance capex vs growth capex: not all capex is the same

In M3-03 you saw how a change in NWC absorbs or releases cash around operating cash flow. We stay on the theme of "how much cash is really available", but move from working capital to investment in fixed assets (capex).

The TOTAL capex spent in a year isn't a single block: it splits into two parts with opposite economic meaning.

- **Maintenance capex**: replaces what wears out (machines that wear, plants that age). It isn't discretionary — it's needed just to stand still, at the same productive capacity.
- **Growth capex**: expands productive capacity (new plants, new lines). It's discretionary — it's done if and when the expected return justifies it.

**The proxy you'll use (stated, not an accounting identity):** the accounts almost never separate the two components. The common, reasonable convention is that in the long run maintenance capex tends to converge towards the year's depreciation (D&A), because D&A measures precisely the consumption of existing assets that maintenance has to replace. It's an approximation, not an equality — but it's the one used when the detail isn't available.

> **Maintenance capex (estimated) = D&A for the year**
> **Growth capex = Total capex − Maintenance capex**

Total capex for the year (given): {p0}. D&A for the year (given): {p1}.

First estimate maintenance capex, then derive growth capex as the difference. High growth capex isn't an alarm: it's optional and should be assessed on its expected return. Maintenance capex, instead, isn't up for negotiation.
M3-04-CAPEXMAINTENANCEGROWTH.8: D&A for the year (proxy for maintenance capex), €
M3-04-CAPEXMAINTENANCEGROWTH.12: ={B_DA}: estimated maintenance capex is simply the year's D&A, by the convention stated in the brief.
M3-04-CAPEXMAINTENANCEGROWTH.13: ={B_CAPEX_TOTALE}-{B_CAPEX_MANT}: total capex minus maintenance capex. What's left is the discretionary slice, spent to grow.
M3-04-CAPEXMAINTENANCEGROWTH.title: Maintenance capex vs growth capex
M3-05-PEGNWC.2: In {B_PEG} compute the NWC peg: the average of the 12 monthly historical NWC values ({B_NWC_START}:{B_NWC_END}). Use an averaging function, don't add up by hand and divide by 12: the peg is, by definition, the average over a FULL YEAR — a complete seasonal cycle — precisely because over 12 full months the months above and below the average offset each other, giving back a "normal" NWC level that doesn't depend on which single month you happen to look at.
M3-05-PEGNWC.3: In {B_SCOSTAMENTO} compute the deviation from the peg: actual NWC at closing ({B_CLOSING}) minus the peg just calculated ({B_PEG}). A POSITIVE result means that at closing NWC is ABOVE the level agreed as normal; a NEGATIVE result means it's BELOW. This number, on its own, isn't yet the price adjustment: the next task turns it into a compensation or a penalty.
M3-05-PEGNWC.4: In {B_AGGIUSTAMENTO} compute the price adjustment for the SELLER: it has THE SAME SIGN as the deviation just calculated ({B_SCOSTAMENTO}) — it must not be flipped. The reason is economic, not just arithmetic: if at closing NWC is ABOVE the peg (positive deviation), the seller has left MORE working capital in the company — more cash, more receivables, more stock net of payables — than agreed as normal, value that passes to the buyer; the price adjusts UPWARDS in the seller's favour (POSITIVE adjustment, a compensation). If instead NWC is BELOW the peg (negative deviation), the seller has left LESS working capital than normal: the buyer will have to top it up out of their own pocket after closing, so the price adjusts DOWNWARDS (NEGATIVE adjustment, a penalty). That's why the adjustment EQUALS the deviation: the temptation to flip its sign, because "an adjustment should correct", is exactly the mistake to avoid here.
M3-05-PEGNWC.5:
## The NWC peg: how much working capital is "normal"?

In an M&A deal, buyer and seller don't know in advance the exact NWC the company will have at the closing date — and neither wants to leave it to chance. So they agree on a "normal" NWC level, the **peg**, BEFORE closing: if actual NWC at closing differs from the peg, the price adjusts. It's the mechanism that protects both sides — from a seller who "squeezes" working capital before selling (doesn't restock, collects everything, doesn't pay suppliers) and from a buyer who demands a discount just because closing happened to fall in a seasonally weak month.

Below you'll find this company's monthly historical NWC for the last year — sales are concentrated around the year-end holidays, so NWC is anything but flat: it grows in the months before the peak (more stock, more receivables from customers) up to the maximum in {meseMax} ({p1}), then falls as Christmas collections come in, down to the minimum in {meseMin} ({p3}).
M3-05-PEGNWC.6:
**The central point**: precisely because NWC swings so much over the year, the NWC of ONE single month would be a terrible benchmark — it would depend on which month you happened to look at. The solution is to use the average over a FULL YEAR, a complete seasonal cycle: over 12 full months the months above and below the average offset each other, leaving a "normal" level that doesn't depend on seasonality. That's how this level calculates the peg: a simple AVERAGE over the 12 months, not a more complex calculation.

Actual NWC at the closing date is {p0}.

Compute the peg (task 1), the deviation of closing NWC from the peg (task 2) and finally the price adjustment for the seller (task 3) — watch the sign of the last one: it equals the deviation, it is NOT its opposite, for the economic reason explained in the task itself.
M3-05-PEGNWC.7: The NWC peg and the price adjustment at closing
M3-05-PEGNWC.16: =AVERAGE({B_NWC_START}:{B_NWC_END}): the average of the 12 monthly values, not a manual sum.
M3-05-PEGNWC.17: ={B_CLOSING}-{B_PEG}: closing NWC minus peg, in that order. Positive = above the peg.
M3-05-PEGNWC.18: ={B_SCOSTAMENTO}: the adjustment has THE SAME SIGN as the deviation, it must not be flipped. NWC above the peg -> positive adjustment (the seller left more value, they're compensated). NWC below the peg -> negative adjustment (the buyer has to top up, the price falls).

M3-07-LOCKEDBOX.5:
## Locked box vs completion accounts: two ways to fix the price

In the peg level you worked with **completion accounts**: price agreed at signing, then adjusted AFTER closing on the real accounts at that date. Until closing the economic risk stays with the seller; the final price is only known weeks later.

The **locked box** turns the scheme around. The equity price is fixed on the accounts of a PAST date, the locked box date (usually the last audited balance sheet): enterprise value minus net debt at that date. From then on the price no longer moves.

From the locked box date **economic risk and benefit pass to the buyer**: if the company does well, the cash generated stays in the company being bought; if it does badly, that's the buyer's problem. But the seller still runs the company until closing, so:

- they must not take value out of it for their own benefit (**leakage**, next level);
- they're compensated with a **ticking fee**: agreed interest on the equity price for the days between locked box date and closing.

Agreed enterprise value: {p0}. Net debt at the locked box date: {p1}. Ticking fee at {p2} a year for {giorni} days.

Compute the equity price, the ticking fee and the amount paid at closing.

M3-08-LEAKAGE.15:
## Leakage: value leaving for the seller's benefit

In the locked box scheme (previous level) the price is fixed at the locked box date and no longer adjusts to the real accounts at closing. But between that date and actual closing the company is still run by the SELLER — and in that window the seller could take value out of the company for their own benefit, before handing it over. That outgoing value is called **leakage**, and locked box contracts regulate it explicitly by distinguishing two cases.

- **Permitted leakage**: agreed in advance in the contract — the seller-manager's ordinary salary, a market rent owed to the seller, a dividend already declared before the locked box date. It's value that would have left anyway, under any owner: it does NOT require compensation.
- **Unpermitted leakage**: everything else — a special dividend declared after the locked box date, the seller's personal expenses paid with company cash, an exceptional management fee to a company of the seller. It's value the buyer never saw and could never count on: it must be repaid to the buyer **euro for euro**, reducing the final price.

The price agreed at signing is {p0} ({p1}). Below you'll find {p2} movements that occurred between the locked box date and closing, each labelled Type = "permitted" or Type = "not permitted", in no particular order.

Adding up the whole list indiscriminately would be a conceptual error, not a detail — exactly the same kind of discipline you already trained in M2 by isolating only the one-off items in a list of legal expenses, or only the legitimate addbacks in a mixed list: the total of ALL movements is {p3}, but only part of that number is unpermitted leakage, and it's that part that reduces the price. Isolate the right rows first, then add up.
